python.name: Python
python.q: What are decorators, generators, and context managers in Python?
python.a: Decorators wrap functions to add cross-cutting behavior (auth, logging). Generators yield lazily, so big data never loads fully into memory. Context managers (`with open(...)`) guarantee cleanup even on errors. I use all three daily in FastAPI/Flask and Frappe hooks.

javascript.name: JavaScript
javascript.q: Explain closures, the event loop, and hoisting in JavaScript.
javascript.a: Closures let an inner function keep access to its outer scope. The event loop pulls callbacks from the message queue only when the call stack is empty, which is how async works. Hoisting moves declarations to the top; `let`/`const` still sit in the temporal dead zone. This underpins everything I write in the browser.

typescript.name: TypeScript
typescript.q: How do generics and type narrowing make code safer?
typescript.a: Generics let one function serve many types with full type-checking; narrowing (`typeof`, `instanceof`, discriminated unions) refines types inside branches. With strict mode, a whole class of runtime bugs becomes compile-time errors. I used it heavily in the Angular and Resume Lens apps.

angular.name: Angular
angular.q: How does change detection work in Angular?
angular.a: Angular re-checks bindings after events. OnPush limits checks to input changes or observable emissions, with manual `ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck` when needed. I pair OnPush with BehaviorSubject + async pipe and got a 25% load-time gain on the sales app.

vue.name: Vue.js
vue.q: Composition API vs Options API — when would you choose each?
vue.a: Composition API (script setup) groups logic by feature with ref/reactive/computed and scales better for complex components. Options API is simpler for tiny components. I default to Composition API for anything non-trivial.

react.name: React
react.q: Explain reconciliation and why keys matter.
react.a: React diffs the virtual DOM against the previous tree and patches only the changed nodes. Keys help it match elements across renders; stable keys prevent unnecessary remounts and state loss. I built a resume-vetting tool in React + TypeScript.

nextjs.name: Next.js
nextjs.q: When do you use SSR, SSG, or ISR in Next.js?
nextjs.a: SSG for content that changes rarely, ISR to revalidate it periodically, SSR for personalized/real-time pages, and client-side fetching for dashboards. I match the rendering strategy to how fresh the data needs to be.

svelte.name: Svelte
svelte.q: What makes Svelte different from React/Vue?
svelte.a: Svelte compiles components into imperative DOM updates at build time, so there's no virtual DOM or runtime framework overhead. That makes bundles smaller and updates faster, at the cost of a slightly different mental model.

nodejs.name: Node.js
nodejs.q: How does the Node.js event loop work?
nodejs.a: Node runs JavaScript on one thread while libuv handles I/O via the event loop (timers, poll, check phases). Blocking sync code stalls the loop, so I keep handlers async and push CPU-heavy work to worker threads or a queue. I build REST APIs on Express and Fastify.

fastapi.name: FastAPI
fastapi.q: What does FastAPI give you over Flask?
fastapi.a: Pydantic validation, automatic OpenAPI docs, and native async. Request/response models are typed and validated at the boundary, so bad payloads fail fast. I use it for clean, self-documenting services.

flask.name: Flask
flask.q: How do you structure a Flask app so it scales?
flask.a: Blueprints per domain, an app factory, and extensions for DB/auth, keeping business logic out of views. I applied this pattern on the e-commerce and HRMS modules so features could be added without tangled routes.

django.name: Django
django.q: When does the Django ORM help, and when does it fight you?
django.a: It maps classes to tables with migrations and a built-in admin — great for CRUD-heavy apps. On complex reporting queries it produces poor SQL, so I drop to raw SQL or views when the plan matters.

go.name: Go / Golang
go.q: Why would you pick Go for a backend service?
go.a: Goroutines make concurrency cheap and readable, compilation produces a single static binary, and the standard library covers HTTP well. For high-throughput services it delivers strong performance with simple deployment.

ruby.name: Ruby on Rails
ruby.q: What are Rails conventions over configuration?
ruby.a: Rails assumes sensible defaults (naming, routes, migrations, MVC layout) so you write less glue. When the convention fits the domain you move fast; when it doesn't, you override deliberately.

java.name: Java / Spring
java.q: What is dependency injection in Spring?
java.a: The container creates and injects beans instead of the class instantiating them — inversion of control. That makes components loosely coupled and easily testable with mocks.

csharp.name: C# / .NET
csharp.q: What are async/await and tasks in C#?
csharp.a: Async/await lets I/O run without blocking a thread — `Task` represents the ongoing operation and the async method resumes when it completes. I use it everywhere in web APIs so the thread pool isn't starved.

cpp.name: C / C++
cpp.q: How does manual memory management work in C++?
cpp.a: `new`/`delete` hand ownership to you, which is error-prone — so modern C++ uses RAII and smart pointers (`unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`) to tie lifetime to scope. When I need raw control, I still prefer containers and RAII wrappers.

kotlin.name: Kotlin
kotlin.q: What makes Kotlin better than Java for Android?
kotlin.a: Null-safety built into the type system, concise data classes, coroutines for async, and full Java interop. It removes whole classes of bugs before they happen and reads far cleaner.

swift.name: Swift / iOS
swift.q: How does SwiftUI differ from UIKit?
swift.a: SwiftUI is declarative — the view is a function of state and the framework diffs updates; UIKit is imperative with explicit view controllers. For new apps SwiftUI is faster to build and test, especially with Swift concurrency.

rust.name: Rust
rust.q: How does Rust guarantee memory safety without a GC?
rust.a: Ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes are checked at compile time: every value has one owner, references are borrowed under strict rules, and the borrow checker rejects unsafe patterns. That eliminates data races and use-after-free while keeping C-like speed.

scala.name: Scala
scala.q: Why does Scala pair well with big data?
scala.a: Functional style maps cleanly onto distributed operations, and it's the native language for Apache Spark. Immutability and strong typing make parallel data pipelines easier to reason about.

rlang.name: R / Statistics
rlang.q: When do you reach for R over Python?
rlang.a: R excels at statistical modeling, hypothesis testing, and rich visualization (ggplot2). For a data analyst's workflow with heavy stats, R's ecosystem is still the strongest.

php.name: PHP
php.q: How do PHP sessions and CSRF protection work?
php.a: Sessions keep state across requests via a server-side store keyed by a cookie. CSRF tokens verify that form submissions originate from the same origin — I always validate tokens server-side on state-changing routes.

sql.name: SQL
sql.q: Write a query to find duplicates in a table.
sql.a: `SELECT col, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY col HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;`. For ranked or deduped results I use window functions, and I always check the plan with EXPLAIN before trusting a query at scale.

postgresql.name: PostgreSQL
postgresql.q: What PostgreSQL features do you rely on most?
postgresql.a: JSONB for flexible documents, full-text search, window functions, and strong MVCC concurrency. I use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to find index and join issues before they reach production.

mysql.name: MySQL
mysql.q: How do you tune a MySQL query?
mysql.a: Add covering indexes for the hot read paths, avoid SELECT *, watch for full table scans in EXPLAIN, and use the slow query log. For big writes I batch them and keep transactions short.

sqlite.name: SQLite
sqlite.q: When is SQLite the right database?
sqlite.a: For single-process apps, embedded storage, prototypes, and local caches where you don't need a server. It's fast, zero-config, and reliable — and it handles surprising amounts of traffic.

oracle.name: Oracle DB
oracle.q: What is PL/SQL and when do you use it?
oracle.a: PL/SQL is Oracle's procedural extension to SQL for server-side logic, triggers, and packages. I use it when logic must run close to the data or cross several tables atomically, but prefer the app layer for complex business rules.

mongodb.name: MongoDB
mongodb.q: When would you choose MongoDB over a relational database?
mongodb.a: Flexible documents, high write throughput, and horizontal scaling. I pick it when the document shape maps directly to the domain. For transactional integrity and complex joins, a relational DB wins.

redis.name: Redis
redis.q: How do you use Redis in a web app?
redis.a: Caching hot reads (sessions, config, computed results) with TTLs, plus queues via lists/streams and rate limiting. Invalidation is the hard part — I version keys and expire aggressively so stale data self-heals.

elasticsearch.name: Elasticsearch
elasticsearch.a: It builds inverted indexes over analyzed text so term lookups are instant. I use it for search and log analytics, designing analyzers and mappings up front and sharding with an eye to the hot cluster.

dynamodb.name: DynamoDB
dynamodb.q: How do you model data in DynamoDB?
dynamodb.a: Single-table design: denormalize access patterns into partition/sort keys so one query returns what you need. You trade joins for predictable latency at scale, so I design the keys around the queries, not the entities.

cassandra.name: Cassandra
cassandra.a: Wide-scale, high-availability writes across nodes with no single point of failure. The catch is query-first modeling — you design tables around your query patterns because secondary indexing is limited.

kafka.name: Kafka
kafka.a: Ordering is guaranteed per partition, not globally. Producers pick a key that routes messages to the same partition, and consumers scale by reading partitions in parallel while the offset marks progress.

rabbitmq.name: RabbitMQ
rabbitmq.q: RabbitMQ vs Kafka — when do you choose which?
rabbitmq.a: RabbitMQ is a smart broker with flexible routing (exchanges, queues, acknowledgments) for task queues; Kafka is a durable log for high-throughput streams. I use RabbitMQ for jobs and Kafka for event streaming at scale.

spark.name: Apache Spark
spark.q: How does Spark process data in memory?
spark.a: RDDs and DataFrames are split into partitions processed in parallel across a cluster, with lazy transformations and eager actions. Caching keeps hot datasets in memory so iterative algorithms avoid re-reading from disk.

airflow.name: Airflow
airflow.q: What is a DAG in Airflow?
airflow.a: A Directed Acyclic Graph of tasks with dependencies, schedules, and retries. Each task is idempotent, so reruns and backfills are safe. I use XComs sparingly and keep tasks small and retryable.

bigquery.name: BigQuery
bigquery.q: Why is BigQuery fast on huge datasets?
bigquery.a: Columnar storage and distributed query execution across thousands of machines, with data clustered and partitioned. You pay per scanned byte, so I prune partitions and select only needed columns.

snowflake.name: Snowflake
snowflake.q: How does Snowflake separate storage from compute?
snowflake.a: Storage and compute scale independently — virtual warehouses spin up per workload and suspend when idle. That lets you run many concurrent queries cheaply without reserving capacity upfront.

docker.name: Docker
docker.a: A Dockerfile defines one image; compose orchestrates containers on a single host; Kubernetes schedules across a cluster. I use multi-stage builds to keep images small and compose for repeatable local dev.

kubernetes.name: Kubernetes
kubernetes.a: A Pod is the smallest schedulable unit. Deployments manage replica counts and rolling updates. Services give stable networking across a pod set, and Ingress routes external traffic. Together they make deployments self-healing.

terraform.name: Terraform
terraform.a: You declare desired state in HCL; Terraform plans the diff and applies it, keeping state to track what it owns. That makes infrastructure reviewable, versionable, and reversible — I treat cloud config like code.

ansible.name: Ansible
ansible.a: Agentless automation over SSH using YAML playbooks — push configuration to servers with idempotent modules. It's simple to start and great for config management, patching, and one-off orchestration.

aws.name: AWS
aws.q: How do you secure an EC2 instance?
aws.a: IAM roles instead of long-lived keys, security groups open only on needed ports, private subnets in a VPC, and encryption at rest. I deployed the ERP on EC2 behind Nginx with automated backups and tested restores.

azure.name: Azure
azure.q: How do Azure resources and resource groups work?
azure.a: Resource groups are logical containers for Azure resources — you apply RBAC, policies, and cost tags at the group level, then deploy apps, databases, and functions into them with ARM/Bicep templates.

gcp.name: Google Cloud
gcp.q: What GCP services do you use for a data-heavy app?
gcp.a: Cloud Run or GKE for compute, BigQuery for analytics, Cloud Storage for objects, and Pub/Sub for events. GCP's data and ML portfolio is where it shines, so I lean on it for pipelines.

firebase.name: Firebase
firebase.q: How do Firestore security rules work?
firebase.a: Rules are evaluated server-side per request and express who can read/write which documents. I write least-privilege rules and validate data shape at the boundary, never trusting client claims.

git.name: Git
git.q: How do you resolve a merge conflict?
git.a: I read both sides and resolve deliberately — never blindly. Feature branches, small PRs, and rebasing onto main keep conflicts rare. When they happen, a quick conversation with the other author usually clarifies intent.

linux.name: Linux
linux.q: How do you diagnose a slow server?
linux.a: Top/free for CPU and memory, df for disk, journalctl for logs, and network checks for latency. I gather metrics, reproduce under load, find the bottleneck, fix it, and verify the improvement.

nginx.name: Nginx
nginx.q: What is Nginx typically used for?
nginx.a: Reverse proxy, TLS termination, static file serving, and load balancing. I put it in front of Gunicorn/Node to handle encryption and serve static assets without tying up app workers.

prometheus.name: Prometheus
prometheus.a: Services expose metrics on an HTTP endpoint and Prometheus scrapes them on a schedule, storing time series with labels. I combine it with Alertmanager and Grafana for alerting and dashboards.

grafana.name: Grafana
grafana.q: How do you build a useful Grafana dashboard?
grafana.a: Start from the SRE golden signals — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — and layer on business metrics. I keep panels focused and annotated so an on-call engineer can read the story in seconds.

frappe.name: Frappe / ERPNext
frappe.q: How do you add a custom field to a DocType safely?
frappe.a: Via the app's custom fields or a dedicated app's JSON, and controllers are overridden through hooks rather than core edits — so framework upgrades don't break my customization. Permissions are enforced at the DocType level.

html.name: HTML & CSS
html.a: Fluid grids, flexible images, and media queries — or modern grid/flexbox. I use Tailwind for utility-first layout and always check accessibility: semantic tags, focus states, and contrast.

tailwind.name: Tailwind CSS
tailwind.q: How do you keep Tailwind classes maintainable?
tailwind.a: Compose reusable components and extract design tokens into the theme config. I use utility-first for layout and spacing, and @apply or component classes for patterns that repeat, so markup stays readable.

webpack.name: Webpack
webpack.q: What is code splitting in webpack?
webpack.a: Splitting the bundle into chunks loaded on demand — route-level or vendor-level — so the initial page ships less JavaScript. I measure with the bundle analyzer and split at natural boundaries.

vite.name: Vite
vite.q: Why is Vite faster than webpack?
vite.a: It serves ES modules directly in dev (no bundling until needed) and pre-bundles dependencies with esbuild. Production builds use Rollup. The instant HMR and startup are why I reach for it by default.

redux.name: Redux
redux.q: When would you add Redux to a React app?
redux.a: When genuinely shared, mutable state spans many components — auth, cart, websocket feeds. Otherwise local state or context is enough. I keep it lean with slices and selectors, and use RTK Query for server state.

graphql.name: GraphQL
graphql.q: How does GraphQL differ from REST?
graphql.a: Clients query exactly the shape they need through a typed schema, reducing over/under-fetching. The cost is caching and complexity, so I add it when clients genuinely need flexible data composition.

websocket.name: WebSockets
websocket.q: When should you use WebSockets over HTTP polling?
websocket.a: For real-time two-way communication — chat, live dashboards, collaborative editing — where polling adds latency and load. WebSockets keep a persistent connection; I add heartbeat and reconnect logic for reliability.

pwa.name: PWA
pwa.q: What makes an app a PWA?
pwa.a: HTTPS, a web app manifest, and a service worker that enables offline caching and background sync. That gives installability and resilience — the app still works on flaky networks.

pandas.name: Pandas
pandas.q: How do you avoid slow Pandas code?
pandas.a: Prefer vectorized operations over iterrows, use the right dtypes, and filter early. For data too big for RAM I chunk it or switch to Polars/Dask. I always profile with .info() and .memory_usage() first.

numpy.name: NumPy
numpy.a: Operations apply to whole arrays at once through compiled C loops instead of Python loops — often 10-100x faster. I express algorithms as array math and let broadcasting handle the shapes.

tensorflow.name: TensorFlow
tensorflow.q: How do you train a model with TensorFlow/Keras?
tensorflow.a: Build a Sequential/Functional model, compile with a loss and optimizer, then fit with validation data and early stopping. I watch the metrics curves for overfitting and iterate on data and architecture.

pytorch.name: PyTorch
pytorch.q: What is a tensor and an autograd graph?
pytorch.a: A tensor is a multi-dimensional array that runs on GPU. Autograd records operations so gradients flow back automatically — you write the forward pass and let it compute backprop.

scikit.name: Scikit-learn
scikit.q: How do you evaluate a classification model?
scikit.a: Split train/test, then look beyond accuracy — precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC — especially on imbalanced data. I use cross-validation and keep a held-out set untouched until final evaluation.

reactnative.name: React Native
reactnative.q: How does React Native share code with web?
reactnative.a: It runs React components on native widgets via a bridge (or JSI), so one codebase targets iOS and Android. Shared business logic and state can live in one place while views adapt per platform.

flutter.name: Flutter
flutter.a: Flutter paints everything itself with the Skia engine and compiles to native code — no bridge. That gives consistent 60/120fps UI across platforms with a single Dart codebase.

electron.name: Electron
electron.q: What are the trade-offs of Electron?
electron.a: It packages Chromium + Node, so web skills build cross-platform desktop apps fast. The cost is memory and bundle size — I keep the main process lean and lazy-load heavy renderers.

wordpress.name: WordPress
wordpress.q: How do you keep WordPress fast?
wordpress.a: Static caching at the edge, optimize images, limit plugins, and lean on the block editor instead of page-builders. I also keep core, themes, and plugins patched and database queries indexed.

rest.name: REST APIs
rest.q: How do you design a clean REST API?
rest.a: Resources as nouns, HTTP verbs for actions, correct status codes, pagination, versioning, and request validation. Writes that can be retried are made idempotent so clients can safely retry on timeout.

microservices.name: Microservices
microservices.a: When teams or release cycles genuinely need independent deploys and scaling. They add real cost — network, consistency, observability — so I start modular/monolithic and split at clear boundaries only.

systemdesign.name: System Design
systemdesign.q: How do you approach a system design problem?
systemdesign.a: Clarify requirements and scale, sketch the data model, then lay out components — API, storage, cache, queues — and reason about bottlenecks. I size for peaks, not averages, and call out single points of failure.

designpatterns.name: Design Patterns
designpatterns.q: Give an example of a design pattern you actually use.
designpatterns.a: The Repository pattern keeps data access behind an interface so swapping SQL for an API or cache doesn't touch business logic. I prefer patterns that reduce coupling over ceremony for its own sake.

oop.name: OOP
oop.q: What are the four pillars of OOP?
oop.a: Encapsulation bundles state with behavior, abstraction hides complexity, inheritance shares behavior, and polymorphism lets one interface serve many types. I use composition first and inherit deliberately.

functional.name: Functional Programming
functional.q: What is a pure function and why care?
functional.a: Same inputs always give same outputs with no side effects, so they're trivially testable, cacheable, and parallel-safe. I keep business logic in pure functions and push side effects to the edges.

testing.name: Testing
testing.q: What makes a good unit test?
testing.a: Isolated, fast, deterministic, and focused on behavior, not implementation. I test the contract — given inputs produce expected outputs — and mock the boundaries like DB and HTTP.

cicd.name: CI/CD
cicd.q: Describe a CI/CD pipeline you would set up.
cicd.a: On push: lint, test, build, scan. Then deploy to staging, run smoke tests, and promote to production behind a feature flag. Rollback is a single command, and secrets live in the CI store, never in the repo.

agile.name: Agile / Scrum
agile.q: How do you run a sprint?
agile.a: Plan the backlog into a sprint, keep stories small and testable, run daily standups to unblock, and end with a review and retrospective. I treat the retro as the most valuable meeting — it drives the actual improvement.

jira.name: Jira
jira.q: How do you keep Jira useful rather than overhead?
jira.a: Keep tickets small, honest, and updated by the team, not the PM alone. I tie work to acceptance criteria and link to PRs so status is visible without meetings.

uiux.name: UI/UX Design
uiux.q: How do you validate a UI design?
uiux.a: Prototype early, test with real users, and measure — task success rate, time-on-task, and satisfaction. I iterate on the highest-impact usability issues before polishing pixels.

figma.name: Figma
figma.q: How do you use Figma in a dev workflow?
figma.a: Design tokens and components in Figma become the source for the frontend's theme, and handoff uses inspect/dev mode. I collaborate in the file so design and code stay in sync.

a11y.name: Accessibility (a11y)
a11y.q: How do you make a web app accessible?
a11y.a: Semantic HTML, keyboard navigability, visible focus, sufficient contrast, and ARIA only where native elements don't cover it. I test with a screen reader and automated axe scans as a baseline.

oauth.name: OAuth / Auth
oauth.q: How does OAuth 2.0 work at a high level?
oauth.a: A client gets a token after the resource owner authorizes it, then presents the token to the API. Scopes limit what the token can do. I use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE for SPAs and short-lived access tokens.

jwt.name: JWT / Sessions
jwt.q: What are the trade-offs of JWT vs server sessions?
jwt.a: JWTs are stateless and scale horizontally without a session store, but revocation is hard and they embed claims. Sessions are revocable but need shared storage. I pick based on whether logout/revocation latency matters.

security.name: Cybersecurity
security.q: How do you harden a web app?
security.a: Input validation and parameterized queries against injection, CSP and secure headers, rate limiting, least-privilege access, and dependency scanning. I treat OWASP Top 10 as a pre-release checklist.

excel.name: Excel / Sheets
excel.q: What do you use Excel/Sheets for beyond tables?
excel.a: Data cleaning, pivot analysis, and quick reporting — and as an integration target for exports/imports in business apps. For repeatable logic I move it into code, but for ad-hoc analysis it's the fastest tool.

powerbi.name: Power BI
powerbi.q: How do you model data in Power BI?
powerbi.a: Star schemas with a fact table and dimensions, relationships defined once, and measures written in DAX. I keep the model simple so reports stay fast and trust the numbers.
